I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the quiet revolution of attention in our hyperconnected age, and what it means to reclaim the interior life.

---

## The Architecture of Attention

We rarely think about attention as a finite resource, yet it may be the most precious commodity we possess. Not money, not time, but attention—the quality of consciousness we bring to bear on the world. Time passes regardless of our engagement with it. Money can be earned, lost, and earned again. But attention, once spent, leaves traces that reshape who we become. We are, in a very real sense, the sum of what we have paid attention to.

This wasn't always so complicated. For most of human history, attention operated within natural constraints. The farmer noticed the weather, the soil, the condition of his livestock. The weaver attended to the thread, the pattern, the tension of the loom. The scholar bent over manuscripts in rooms lit by flickering candles, the very material difficulty of reading ensuring that attention was consecrated, made solemn by effort. Distraction existed, certainly—the neighbor's conversation, the crying child, the bird at the window—but these interruptions were embodied, localized, comprehensible within the sensory field.

Something fundamental shifted with the digitization of attention. The smartphone in your pocket represents perhaps the most sophisticated attention-harvesting device ever created, more efficient than television, more insidious than advertising, more relentless than any previous technology of distraction. It operates through what we might call the economics of intermittent reinforcement—the same psychological mechanism that makes slot machines addictive. We check our phones not because we expect reward every time, but because we *might* receive reward. A message from someone we love. A piece of validating news. A moment of novelty in the gray fabric of routine. The unpredictability is the point.

What we have built, collectively, is an attention economy that treats human consciousness as extractable resource. The platforms that mediate so much of modern life are not designed to serve your flourishing. They are designed to maximize engagement, which is a different thing entirely. Engagement does not discriminate between the nourishment of genuine interest and the compulsion of anxiety, outrage, or boredom. A mind that flits between stimuli, never settling, never deepening, is in many ways the ideal consumer of digital content. The shallow skimmer generates more ad impressions than the deep reader.

I want to be careful here not to lapse into simple technopessimism. The same networks that fragment attention also enable genuine connection, access to knowledge, creative collaboration across distance. I have learned extraordinary things from strangers on the internet. I have witnessed moments of collective witnessing—deaths of public figures, natural disasters, shared celebrations—that have a quality of genuine human solidarity. The technology is not monolithic. But its default settings, the path of least resistance it creates, tends toward the fragmentation of attention into ever-smaller units. The scroll is infinite. The notification is eternal. The next thing is always more interesting than this thing, because it is not yet known.

---

## The Lost Art of Boredom

We have, as a culture, become intolerant of boredom. This is a profound loss, though it sounds paradoxical to say so. Boredom—the state of being understimulated, of having to endure the friction of time passing without adequate distraction—has historically been the crucible of creativity. The mind, denied easy entertainment, begins to entertain itself. It makes connections, tells stories, imagines alternatives. The bored child becomes a world-builder. The bored adult begins to notice what has been overlooked.

Consider the spaces where boredom once lived: the waiting room, the bus stop, the queue at the post office, the long evening without plans. These have been systematically colonized by the smartphone. Every interstice of the day, every gap between activities, can now be filled with content. The result is a kind of temporal monoculture, where all moments aspire to the same density of stimulation. We have lost the fallow periods in which the mind restores itself, the empty spaces from which unexpected growth emerges.

There is neurological research suggesting that the "default mode network" of the brain—active during periods of rest and mind-wandering—plays crucial roles in memory consolidation, self-reflection, and creative problem-solving. When we fill every empty moment with external input, we may be actively suppressing the brain's capacity for its most integrative work. The mind needs to wander to find its way home to itself.

I think often of the artist Agnes Martin, who spent long periods in the desert, painting grids that seem to contain infinite stillness. Or of the writer Jenny Odell, who advocates for "doing nothing" as a form of political resistance against the attention economy. These are not calls to laziness but to a different kind of activity—the difficult, rewarding work of being present without purpose, of attending to the world without extracting value from it.

---

## Depth and Its Discontents

The opposite of attention is not merely distraction but shallowness—the quality of experience that skims across surfaces without penetrating to interiority. We live in an age of unprecedented access to information and, I would argue, unprecedented difficulty in achieving genuine understanding. The problem is not that knowledge is unavailable but that it arrives already contextualized by the systems that deliver it, optimized for engagement rather than education, for reaction rather than reflection.

Consider reading a book versus reading about a book. The former requires sustained attention, the building of mental models across hundreds of pages, the tolerance of confusion and slow revelation. The latter offers immediate gratification: the plot summary, the critical consensus, the position one might take in conversation. Social media is full of people who have opinions about books they haven't read, films they haven't watched, ideas they haven't encountered in their original form. This is not stupidity but adaptation to an environment that rewards the appearance of cultural participation over its substance.

The philosopher Byung-Chul Han writes about "the burnout society," where subjects become self-exploiters, driven by internalized achievement pressure. I think we might also speak of "the skim society," where the optimal strategy is to sample widely rather than engage deeply, to accumulate references rather than develop expertise. The cost is a kind of experiential poverty: the person who has watched the beginning of ten television series but finished none, who follows the news constantly without understanding any issue's history, who has opinions about everything and convictions about nothing.

There is something existentially unsettling about this shallowness. The self that skims is not a stable self. It is a continuous present without the ballast of memory, without the coherence that comes from sustained commitment to particular objects of attention. We become, in the philosopher Martin Heidegger's terms, lost in the "they-self"—the anonymous public opinion that thinks for us, feels for us, decides what matters.

---

## Reclaiming Attention

If attention is the scarce resource, then its cultivation becomes a kind of ethical practice. Not a matter of productivity hacks or mindfulness apps—many of which are themselves products of the attention economy, offering to solve the problem they participate in creating—but of deliberate, often difficult choices about how to inhabit time.

For me, this has meant reclaiming specific practices that resist the logic of the feed. Long-form reading, certainly—books that demand hours or days, that change the rhythm of thought to match their own. But also conversation without phones present, the kind of dialogue that wanders and deepens and returns to itself. Walking without podcasts, letting the mind move with the body. The deliberate cultivation of boredom, the refusal to fill every waiting moment.

I have come to value what I call "attentional loyalty"—the choice to return to the same object of attention across time, to develop a relationship with it rather than consuming it and moving on. This is how I have come to love certain pieces of music, returning to them across years, finding new layers with each listening. It is how I have maintained friendships that require patience and forgiveness, that do not offer the immediate dopamine of novelty but something more durable.

There is also the practice of attention to the non-human world, which offers a peculiar kind of restoration. The tree outside my window does not want my engagement. It does not optimize for my attention. It simply exists, indifferent to my notice, and in this indifference there is relief from the exhausting reciprocity of social media, where every glance is tracked, every interaction monetized. The natural world offers attention without transaction, a form of contemplation that is not being harvested for someone else's profit.

---

## The Politics of Attention

I want to suggest, finally, that attention is not merely personal but political. The attention economy is not a neutral technology but a system of power, shaping what can be thought and who can think it. When public discourse is conducted through platforms designed to maximize engagement, certain kinds of thought become difficult or impossible. Nuance does not engage. Complexity does not engage. The slow building of trust across difference does not engage. What engages is outrage, simplification, the identification of enemies, the performance of moral superiority.

This has consequences for our collective capacity to address complex problems. Climate change requires sustained attention to systems that operate across timescales longer than any news cycle. Social inequality requires understanding historical patterns that resist condensation into viral content. Democracy requires the tolerance of disagreement, the willingness to hold multiple perspectives in mind simultaneously—cognitive work that is actively undermined by platforms that reward the most polarizing voices.

To reclaim attention, then, is not merely self-care but a form of civic participation. It is to insist on the value of thinking that cannot be reduced to content, of relationships that cannot be monetized, of presence that cannot be captured in data. It is to resist the colonization of consciousness by forces that do not have our flourishing in mind.

---

## Toward a Slow Ethics

I do not have a program to offer, a set of techniques guaranteed to restore attention in an age of distraction. The forces arrayed against attention are powerful, well-funded, and embedded in the infrastructure of daily life. Individual solutions—digital detoxes, app blockers, the purchase of a flip phone—can be helpful but also feel like a kind of luxury good, available to those with sufficient privilege to opt out of systems that others depend upon for economic survival or social connection.

What I can imagine is something more collective: a slow ethics that recognizes attention as shared resource, as commons to be protected rather than exploited. This would mean designing technologies that respect cognitive limits rather than exploiting them. It would mean valuing education that teaches attention as skill, the way we teach literacy or numeracy. It would mean creating public spaces—physical and temporal—that protect against extraction, where presence is not a commodity.

More personally, it would mean the difficult work of choosing, again and again, depth over breadth, presence over productivity, the difficult real over the easy virtual. It would mean accepting the discomfort of not knowing, of not being entertained, of not being validated—trusting that something emerges from this discomfort that is more valuable than the immediate relief of distraction.

I think of the writer Annie Dillard, who spent a year at Tinker Creek, watching, waiting, attending to the smallest movements of water and light. "How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives," she wrote. The days of attention are not easy. They require saying no to much that is tempting, convenient, socially expected. But they accumulate into a life of a different quality—one in which we are present to our own experience, capable of genuine encounter with others, able to think thoughts that require more than a moment to unfold.

The attention economy will not last forever. No system of exploitation does. What replaces it depends on what we imagine and practice now, in the small choices of daily life, in the quiet refusal to let our most intimate capacities be sold to the highest bidder. The revolution begins in the decision to look away from the screen, to endure the initial discomfort, to discover what waits in the space we have cleared. It begins in the recognition that attention is not merely a means to an end but the very medium of our being, the quality of light in which we come to know ourselves and the world.

This is the work of a lifetime, never finished, always beginning again. But it is, I believe, the most important work we can do—to become, in an age of fragmentation, people capable of wholeness, of presence, of the deep attention that is the foundation of love and understanding and any world we might want to inhabit.

---
